title: The relationship between cognitive performance on generic cognitive tests and a sport themed reaction time test
content:
by Tess L. Rolley, Natalie Saunders, Alicia Goodwill, Brendan Major, Sandy Shultz, Aaron S. Fox

In sport, generic cognitive tests are used to assess baseline cognitive function and monitor concussion. The understanding of how performance on these generic cognitive tests relates to sport-specific cognitive performance is unknown. This study assessed relationships between cognitive performance on generic cognitive tests versus a sport-themed reaction time (RT) test. Twenty (mean±SD, age = 24 ± 6years; height = 169.15 ± 6.21 cm; mass = 66.50 ± 7.92 kg) women’s Australian-rules football players participated. The tests included: (i) Deary Liewald; (ii) one-back; (iii) four-choice reaction time; (iv) two-back; (v) one-card learning; and, (vi) three-back. The sport-themed RT test replicated a reactive defending scenario with the participant responding to an attacking opponent changing direction. Performance accuracy and reaction time for correct responses were assessed for all tests, with balanced integration scores calculated to describe overall speed-accuracy performance. Pearson’s r correlations were used to explore the strength and statistical significance (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted alpha of 0.05) of relationships between the generic cognitive and sport themed RT tests. A statistically significant correlation (r = 0.618, p = 0.005, CI: 0.230–0.840) for correct reaction time was found between the four-choice reaction time test and the sport-themed RT test suggesting generic cognitive tests of similar nature (i.e., filtering of multiple cues) relates closely to reactions to sport-specific cognitive stimuli. With one statistically significant relationship found between generic cognitive tests to a sport-themed test, this suggests future research is required to improve the ecological validity of cognitive testing in sport.
